The work was written by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (1789‑1866), the third Lubavitcher Rebbe, who was known as the *Tzemach Tzedek*.  
He grew up under the direct guidance of his maternal grandfather, **Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi**, the founder of the Chabad‑Lubavitch movement.  As a young man he studied closely with his grandfather and absorbed the Chassidic teaching of the Chabad “branch” that his grandfather had established.  Thus, the creator of *Derech Mitzvosecha* followed the spiritual and intellectual tradition of his grandfather, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Derech Mitzvosecha (Sefer Hamitzvos)   
_Derech Mitzvosecha_, 1912 edition  
Author Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn ("Tzemach Tzedek"), the third Rebbe of Chabad  
Language Hebrew  
Subject Jewish mysticism, Chabad philosophy  
Genre non-fiction  
Published 7x10 Hardcover, 570pp, (Kehot Publication Society, Brooklyn New York)  
ISBN0826655904
_**Derech Mitzvosecha**_, also titled _**Sefer Hamitzvos**_ (Hebrew: דרך מצותך: ספר המצות), is an interpretive work on the Jewish commandments authored by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (1789–1866), the third Rebbe of the ChabadHasidic movement. The work is considered a fundamental text of Chabad philosophy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2)

## Interpretation of the commandments
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_, Rabbi Menachem Mendel interprets the Jewish commandments ("mitzvos") according to Kabbalistic and Hasidic teachings. Topics include the commandments of belief in God, prayer, love of a fellow Jew, Tzitzit (fringes on four cornered garments) and Tefillin (phylacteries), and many others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2) The work provides a Hasidic perspective on fundamental Jewish rites and observances.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-3)
In some cases, Rabbi Menachem Mendel seeks to clarify or reconcile earlier rabbinic interpretations of the commandments, especially where earlier rabbinic authorities disagree on the matter. In this regard, Hasidic interpretations are employed to refine the statements of earlier authorities and/or to clarify or resolve their differences.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-4)

## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_ Rabbi Menachem Mendel discusses the commandment to love one's fellow and not to hate him/her[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-5) and questions the story in the Talmud concerning Hillel the Elder and the convert. Hillel instructed a non-Jew wishing to convert "what to you is hateful do not do to your friend, this is the (root of) the entire Torah, the rest is commentary. Go and learn."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-6)
For Rabbi Menachem Mendel, the idea of loving one's fellow should only be considered the root of all commandments that relate to human interactions, "between man and his friend" (_bein adam l'chaveiro_), but not to those that are "between man and God" (_bein adam l'makom_).
Rabbi Menachem Mendel resolves this question by introducing the Kabbalistic idea that the souls of the Jewish people compose a "single body"; each individual represents a particular limb.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-7) Based on this concept, every Jew is obligated to love their fellow though the other may have some deficiency, just as the individual often overlooks their own faults due to the natural love one has for one's self. When this kind of "self love" is extended to each other person, it achieves a very strong unity of spirit.
According to Rabbi Menachem Mendel, this unity is representative of the unity between God and the Jewish people and is the root of all the commandments, for aside from the specifics of the individual commandment, each serve the additional function of uniting the Jews with God. Thus each commandment may be said to be the "commentary" of the commandment to love one's fellow.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-8)

## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
Rabbi Menachem Mendel published few of his works during his lifetime. The first edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was in Poltava (current day Ukraine), 1912-1913.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-9) Later editions were published by Kehot Publication Society in Brooklyn, New York.
An English edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was translated by Rabbi Eliyahu Touger and published in 2004 by the Chabad publishing house Sichos in English. The English edition translates selected chapters from Rabbi Schneersohn's work.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-10)
The Kehot editions include a number of appendices in the work, including _Kitzur Tanya_, a summary of the _Tanya_, the classic Chabad work by Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.

### Love of another Jew

The Chasidic classic Derech Mitzvosecha, by Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch also known as the Tzemach Tzedek, the third Lubavitcher Rebbe (5549 [1789] – 5626 [1866]) translated to English.
R. Menachem Mendel composed this work in his early adulthood. It focuses on many of the 613 mitzvos of the Torah. The Tzemach Tzedek begins his treatment of each mitzvah by quoting the Sefer Hachinuch, the landmark work that lists all 613 mitzvos and their motivating rationales. Occasionally, it cites other sources in Nigleh and briefly outlines the mystical secrets the Kabbalah associates with this Mitzvah. afterwards, he explains these ideas within the context of Chassidus and in the course of doing so, provides his readers with many fundamental concepts applicable in their Divine service.

Derech Mitzvotecha dives into reasons behind mitzvot such as tzitzit, tefillin, prayer, belief in G-d, loving a fellow Jew, starting a family and many others. Derech Mitzvosecha (Sefer Hamitzvos)   
_Derech Mitzvosecha_, 1912 edition  
Author Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn ("Tzemach Tzedek"), the third Rebbe of Chabad  
Language Hebrew  
Subject Jewish mysticism, Chabad philosophy  
Genre non-fiction  
Published 7x10 Hardcover, 570pp, (Kehot Publication Society, Brooklyn New York)  
ISBN0826655904
_**Derech Mitzvosecha**_, also titled _**Sefer Hamitzvos**_ (Hebrew: דרך מצותך: ספר המצות), is an interpretive work on the Jewish commandments authored by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (1789–1866), the third Rebbe of the ChabadHasidic movement. The work is considered a fundamental text of Chabad philosophy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2)
texts.1:
## Interpretation of the commandments
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_, Rabbi Menachem Mendel interprets the Jewish commandments ("mitzvos") according to Kabbalistic and Hasidic teachings. Topics include the commandments of belief in God, prayer, love of a fellow Jew, Tzitzit (fringes on four cornered garments) and Tefillin (phylacteries), and many others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2) The work provides a Hasidic perspective on fundamental Jewish rites and observances.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-3)
In some cases, Rabbi Menachem Mendel seeks to clarify or reconcile earlier rabbinic interpretations of the commandments, especially where earlier rabbinic authorities disagree on the matter. In this regard, Hasidic interpretations are employed to refine the statements of earlier authorities and/or to clarify or resolve their differences.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-4)
texts.2:
## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_ Rabbi Menachem Mendel discusses the commandment to love one's fellow and not to hate him/her[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-5) and questions the story in the Talmud concerning Hillel the Elder and the convert. Hillel instructed a non-Jew wishing to convert "what to you is hateful do not do to your friend, this is the (root of) the entire Torah, the rest is commentary. Go and learn."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-6)
For Rabbi Menachem Mendel, the idea of loving one's fellow should only be considered the root of all commandments that relate to human interactions, "between man and his friend" (_bein adam l'chaveiro_), but not to those that are "between man and God" (_bein adam l'makom_).
Rabbi Menachem Mendel resolves this question by introducing the Kabbalistic idea that the souls of the Jewish people compose a "single body"; each individual represents a particular limb.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-7) Based on this concept, every Jew is obligated to love their fellow though the other may have some deficiency, just as the individual often overlooks their own faults due to the natural love one has for one's self. When this kind of "self love" is extended to each other person, it achieves a very strong unity of spirit.
According to Rabbi Menachem Mendel, this unity is representative of the unity between God and the Jewish people and is the root of all the commandments, for aside from the specifics of the individual commandment, each serve the additional function of uniting the Jews with God. Thus each commandment may be said to be the "commentary" of the commandment to love one's fellow.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-8)
texts.3:
## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
Rabbi Menachem Mendel published few of his works during his lifetime. The first edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was in Poltava (current day Ukraine), 1912-1913.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-9) Later editions were published by Kehot Publication Society in Brooklyn, New York.
An English edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was translated by Rabbi Eliyahu Touger and published in 2004 by the Chabad publishing house Sichos in English. The English edition translates selected chapters from Rabbi Schneersohn's work.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-10)
The Kehot editions include a number of appendices in the work, including _Kitzur Tanya_, a summary of the _Tanya_, the classic Chabad work by Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.

**Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** (Yiddish: מנחם מענדל שניאורסאהן; September 20, 1789 – March 17, 1866), also known as the **Tzemach Tzedek** (Hebrew: "Righteous Sprout" or "Righteous Scion"), was an Orthodoxrabbi, leading 19th-century posek, and the third Rebbe (spiritual leader) of the Chabad LubavitchHasidic movement.

Menachem Mendel Schneersohn was born in Liozna, on September 20, 1789 (September 9 OS). His mother Devorah Leah died three years later, and her father Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi raised him as his own son. He married his first cousin Chaya Mushka Schneersohn, daughter of Rabbi Dovber Schneuri. After his father-in-law/uncle's death, and a three-year interregnum during which he tried to persuade the Hasidim to accept his brother-in-law Menachem-Nachum Schneuri or his uncle Chaim-Avraham as their leader,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) he assumed the leadership of Lubavitch on the eve of Shavuot 5591 (May 5, 1831, OS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-2)
He was known as the Tzemach Tzedek after the title of a voluminous compendium of Halakha (Jewish law) that he authored.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-3) He also authored _Derech Mitzvotecha_ ("Way of Your Commandments"), a mystical exposition of the _Mitzvos_. He compiled major works of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi for publication, including the _Siddur L'Kol Ha'Shanah_ (commonly known as _Siddur Im Dach_), _Likutei Torah_ and _Torah Ohr_. He also authored a philosophical text entitled _Sefer HaChakira: Derech Emunah_ (_Book of Philosophy: The Way of Faith_).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-4)

He enjoyed close ties with other Jewish leaders. In the course of his battle against the _Haskalah_ in Russia, he forged a close alliance with Rabbi Yitzchak of Valozhyn, a major leader of the misnagdim, which led to warmer relations between them and the Hasidim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-5)
According to Baruch Epstein, his father Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein spent six months under the Schneersohn's tutelage, and learned most of his mystical knowledge during that time. This story is disputed by Hassidic historian Yehoshua Mondshine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-6) Historian [Eitam Henkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Eitam_and_Na'ama_Henkin "Murder of Eitam and Na'ama Henkin") suggests that Rabbi Y. M. **Rabbi Menachem Mendel bar Sholom Shachna of Lubavitch**Yahrzeit - **13 Nissan**Resting place - **Lubavitch, Smolensk Region**The Rebbe's mother, who was born on the eve of Rosh Hashanah 5549 (1789), was Devorah Leah, daughter of the founder of Chabad Chassidism, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi (1745-1812). Rebbetzin Devorah Leah passed away three days after Menachem Mendel's third birthday, after which the orphaned child was raised by his illustrious grandfather.

The boy displayed astonishing abilities from a very early age. By the age of twelve he had already authored numerous scholarly works on questions of Halacha and was recording the Talmudic and Chassidic teachings of his grandfather, supplementing them with his own commentaries and explanations. Long before he turned twenty, Rabbi Schneur Zalman invited him to take part in conducting the necessary research and writing responsa to the numerous halachic inquiries pouring in from various Talmudic scholars across Russia and Europe.When Rabbi Menachem Mendel was only eighteen, his grandfather discovered the manuscript of his famous discourse "The Roots of the Commandment of Prayer" ("Shoresh Mitzvat HaTefillah"), which the young man had been trying to keep hidden from everyone. Rabbi Schneur Zalman was so pleased with his find that he subsequently devoted far more time to studying together with his grandson. And when Rabbi Menachem Mendel was just twenty years old, he was appointed to oversee all of Rabbi Schneur Zalman's communal affairs.After the passing of Rabbi Schneur Zalman (1813), he was succeeded by his son, Rabbi Dovber (uncle and father-in-law of Rabbi Menachem Mendel). It was then that Rabbi Menachem Mendel began a fourteen-year period of seclusion, which lasted fourteen years. These years of solitude were devoted to study and prayer. In 1826, when Rabbi Dovber was accused of "subversive" activity, Rabbi Menachem Mendel began to take part in public affairs, and his first undertaking was organizing a committee to defend Rabbi Dovber. When Rabbi Dovber passed away in 1827, the Chassidim turned to Rabbi Menachem Mendel and asked him to lead the Chabad-Lubavitch movement. It took him many months to decide to take on the enormous responsibility that came with this position, but in the end he accepted the offer.Rabbi Menachem Mendel was a very prolific writer. His works represent a unique synthesis of the "esoteric" and "exoteric" aspects of Torah — reflections on the Talmud, Midrash, Kabbalah, and Chassidism coexist harmoniously and naturally, complementing one another. He would, of course, have preferred to write and edit the works of his grandfather and father-in-law rather than lead the tens of thousands who had joined the ranks of the Lubavitch movement.

But the era brought new challenges. Jews in Russia were barred from many professions, including certain kinds of business activity, and poverty was spreading. Rabbi Menachem Mendel was deeply concerned with strengthening the economic position of the empire's Jewish population, and accordingly advised the Chassidim to take up farming wherever possible, even providing financial assistance to those who followed his advice.Settling in villages was not easy for Jews in those days, so the Rebbe purchased a large plot of land near Minsk and settled a large group of Jewish families there. In 1844 he acquired from Prince Shchedrinov another plot of land with forests in Minsk province. Thus the settlement of Shchedrin was founded, and the Rebbe established a council to administer it.The founding of Shchedrin made a profound impression on both Jews and non-Jews. A report written by an official of Minsk province to the Minister of Internal Affairs speaks of Rabbi Schneerson of Lubavitch with respect and reverence. The document notes that by founding the settlement on the acquired land, the Rebbe improved the living conditions and economic situation of the Jews, and it also mentions the Lubavitcher Rabbi's powerful influence over all the Jews of the "Jewish Pale of Settlement of the Russian Empire" and his efforts to improve their material conditions.In 1827 Nicholas I issued a decree on "cantonists," under which children from the age of twelve began to be conscripted into the army. Under a set quota, Jewish communities were required to supply ten recruits per thousand people (the quota for non-Jews was lower, and it was easier for them to exempt their children from conscription). The conscripted children were assigned by government officials — either placed in peasant homes or sent to special schools, where they remained until the age of eighteen, after which they were transferred to barracks, where they were required to serve for the next twenty-five years. This meant that children were torn away from home and cheder for a very long time, deliberately alienated from their people.No parent would willingly subject their child to such a cruel ordeal, but the community was obligated to fulfill the quota. This gave rise to the despicable trade of the "khapers" (catchers), whose job was to seize or kidnap children and hand them over to government officials. Heartbreaking scenes in which children were literally torn from their mothers' arms became commonplace.

It was especially hard on the poorer segments of the Jewish population, who had no means to buy their children's freedom from the "khapers."Rabbi Menachem Mendel took up this problem with great energy, disregarding the possible threats and danger of the situation. It was necessary to save as many already-conscripted children as possible. To this end, the Rebbe formed a special council whose tasks were:1. To examine the situation of each Jewish community in order to help reduce the number of children it was required to send into military service.2. To take part in freeing children who had already been seized. This task was carried out by a secret society known as "Tachiyat HaMeitim" ("Reviving the Dead"). The main method of securing release was paying ransom to the officials involved in the matter. The latter would return the children while reporting to the authorities that they had died en route, and would also inform the relevant community of the boy's "death." These "death certificates" brought parents indescribable joy. The "deceased," of course, had to be hidden for a long time (hence the society's name), after which they were sent off to Talmud Torahs far from their home towns.3. To send trustworthy people to the places where the cantonist children were stationed, whose task was to offer them moral support and encourage them to remain faithful to their religion and their people.This activity involved not only enormous expense but also great danger, since it was tantamount to treason against the state. Nevertheless, this underground program was carried out successfully, and not a single case of betrayal was ever recorded.At the same time, Rabbi Menachem Mendel focused his efforts on supporting agricultural centers in the Vitebsk and Minsk areas. He sent one of the leading figures of the Chassidic movement, Rabbi Hillel of Paritch, on a tour of the settlements in the Kherson region.

## Tzemach Tzedek - R' Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch
Item Number:EY-TZEM
Detailed Description  
**By:** Rabbi Sholom DovBer Avtzon
**Format:** 6" x 9" Hardcover, 576 Pages
**Language:** English
**The Rebbeim Biography Series - The life of the Rebbe The Tzemach Tzedek**
In order to save the life of her father, the Alter Rebbe, and the teachings of Chasidut, Rebbetzin Devorah Leah gave up her life. Fulfilling her final request, the Alter Rebbe raised her young orphaned son, Menachem Mendel.
Encouraged by his illustrious grandfather to write his own Torah thoughts, the Tzemach Tzedek became known for his prolific writings in Chasidut and Halachah. In his unique style, he combined the two dimensions of Chasidut and Nigleh into one. Similarly, during his lifetime, he brought about an unprecedented unity between the chasidim and misnagdim.
When he agreed to become the third Rebbe of Lubavitch, the Tzemach Tzedek stipulated that his leadership be limited to teaching and guiding the Chasidim. But when the Czar`s tyrannical decrees threatened Jewish education and the Jewish way of life throughout Russia, he rose to battle for the survival of Russian Jewry.
The Tzemach Tzedek tirelessly combated the Enlightenment (Haskalah) Movement and set up underground networks to help the Cantonist soldiers maintain their Jewish identity. Single-handedly, he derailed the Czar`s insidious plans to wreak havoc on Jewish life.
Establishing agricultural communities, finding livelihoods for tens of thousands of Jewish families, setting up chadorim throughout Russia helping agunot were just some of his many accomplishments. His devotion and concern were directed to every Jew, chasid and non-chasid alike.
It is an honor to present the third volume in the _The Rebbeim Biography Series_. By reading about the Tzemach Tzedek`s actions, teachings and conduct - many presented here in English for the first time - may we become connected to him and emulate his ways.

**Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** (Yiddish: מנחם מענדל שניאורסאהן; September 20, 1789 – March 17, 1866), also known as the **Tzemach Tzedek** (Hebrew: "Righteous Sprout" or "Righteous Scion"), was an Orthodoxrabbi, leading 19th-century posek, and the third Rebbe (spiritual leader) of the Chabad LubavitchHasidic movement.

His mother Devorah Leah died three years later, and her father Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi raised him as his own son. He married his first cousin Chaya Mushka Schneersohn, daughter of Rabbi Dovber Schneuri. After his father-in-law/uncle's death, and a three-year interregnum during which he tried to persuade the Hasidim to accept his brother-in-law Menachem-Nachum Schneuri or his uncle Chaim-Avraham as their leader,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) he assumed the leadership of Lubavitch on the eve of Shavuot 5591 (May 5, 1831, OS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-2)

He compiled major works of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi for publication, including the _Siddur L'Kol Ha'Shanah_ (commonly known as _Siddur Im Dach_), _Likutei Torah_ and _Torah Ohr_. He also authored a philosophical text entitled _Sefer HaChakira: Derech Emunah_ (_Book of Philosophy: The Way of Faith_).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-4)

## Tzemach Tzedek - R' Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch
Item Number:EY-TZEM
Detailed Description  
**By:** Rabbi Sholom DovBer Avtzon
**Format:** 6" x 9" Hardcover, 576 Pages
**Language:** English
**The Rebbeim Biography Series - The life of the Rebbe The Tzemach Tzedek**
In order to save the life of her father, the Alter Rebbe, and the teachings of Chasidut, Rebbetzin Devorah Leah gave up her life. Fulfilling her final request, the Alter Rebbe raised her young orphaned son, Menachem Mendel.
Encouraged by his illustrious grandfather to write his own Torah thoughts, the Tzemach Tzedek became known for his prolific writings in Chasidut and Halachah. In his unique style, he combined the two dimensions of Chasidut and Nigleh into one. Similarly, during his lifetime, he brought about an unprecedented unity between the chasidim and misnagdim.
When he agreed to become the third Rebbe of Lubavitch, the Tzemach Tzedek stipulated that his leadership be limited to teaching and guiding the Chasidim. But when the Czar`s tyrannical decrees threatened Jewish education and the Jewish way of life throughout Russia, he rose to battle for the survival of Russian Jewry.
The Tzemach Tzedek tirelessly combated the Enlightenment (Haskalah) Movement and set up underground networks to help the Cantonist soldiers maintain their Jewish identity. Single-handedly, he derailed the Czar`s insidious plans to wreak havoc on Jewish life.
Establishing agricultural communities, finding livelihoods for tens of thousands of Jewish families, setting up chadorim throughout Russia helping agunot were just some of his many accomplishments. His devotion and concern were directed to every Jew, chasid and non-chasid alike.
It is an honor to present the third volume in the _The Rebbeim Biography Series_. By reading about the Tzemach Tzedek`s actions, teachings and conduct - many presented here in English for the first time - may we become connected to him and emulate his ways.
* * *

texts.0: **Rabbi Menachem Mendel bar Sholom Shachna of Lubavitch**Yahrzeit - **13 Nissan**Resting place - **Lubavitch, Smolensk Region**The Rebbe's mother, who was born on the eve of Rosh Hashanah 5549 (1789), was Devorah Leah, daughter of the founder of Chabad Chassidism, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi (1745-1812). Rebbetzin Devorah Leah passed away three days after Menachem Mendel's third birthday, after which the orphaned child was raised by his illustrious grandfather.
texts.1: The boy displayed astonishing abilities from a very early age. By the age of twelve he had already authored numerous scholarly works on questions of Halacha and was recording the Talmudic and Chassidic teachings of his grandfather, supplementing them with his own commentaries and explanations. Long before he turned twenty, Rabbi Schneur Zalman invited him to take part in conducting the necessary research and writing responsa to the numerous halachic inquiries pouring in from various Talmudic scholars across Russia and Europe.When Rabbi Menachem Mendel was only eighteen, his grandfather discovered the manuscript of his famous discourse "The Roots of the Commandment of Prayer" ("Shoresh Mitzvat HaTefillah"), which the young man had been trying to keep hidden from everyone. Rabbi Schneur Zalman was so pleased with his find that he subsequently devoted far more time to studying together with his grandson. And when Rabbi Menachem Mendel was just twenty years old, he was appointed to oversee all of Rabbi Schneur Zalman's communal affairs.After the passing of Rabbi Schneur Zalman (1813), he was succeeded by his son, Rabbi Dovber (uncle and father-in-law of Rabbi Menachem Mendel). It was then that Rabbi Menachem Mendel began a fourteen-year period of seclusion, which lasted fourteen years. These years of solitude were devoted to study and prayer. In 1826, when Rabbi Dovber was accused of "subversive" activity, Rabbi Menachem Mendel began to take part in public affairs, and his first undertaking was organizing a committee to defend Rabbi Dovber. When Rabbi Dovber passed away in 1827, the Chassidim turned to Rabbi Menachem Mendel and asked him to lead the Chabad-Lubavitch movement. It took him many months to decide to take on the enormous responsibility that came with this position, but in the end he accepted the offer.Rabbi Menachem Mendel was a very prolific writer. His works represent a unique synthesis of the "esoteric" and "exoteric" aspects of Torah — reflections on the Talmud, Midrash, Kabbalah, and Chassidism coexist harmoniously and naturally, complementing one another. He would, of course, have preferred to write and edit the works of his grandfather and father-in-law rather than lead the tens of thousands who had joined the ranks of the Lubavitch movement.
texts.2: But the era brought new challenges. Jews in Russia were barred from many professions, including certain kinds of business activity, and poverty was spreading. Rabbi Menachem Mendel was deeply concerned with strengthening the economic position of the empire's Jewish population, and accordingly advised the Chassidim to take up farming wherever possible, even providing financial assistance to those who followed his advice.Settling in villages was not easy for Jews in those days, so the Rebbe purchased a large plot of land near Minsk and settled a large group of Jewish families there. In 1844 he acquired from Prince Shchedrinov another plot of land with forests in Minsk province. Thus the settlement of Shchedrin was founded, and the Rebbe established a council to administer it.The founding of Shchedrin made a profound impression on both Jews and non-Jews. A report written by an official of Minsk province to the Minister of Internal Affairs speaks of Rabbi Schneerson of Lubavitch with respect and reverence. The document notes that by founding the settlement on the acquired land, the Rebbe improved the living conditions and economic situation of the Jews, and it also mentions the Lubavitcher Rabbi's powerful influence over all the Jews of the "Jewish Pale of Settlement of the Russian Empire" and his efforts to improve their material conditions.In 1827 Nicholas I issued a decree on "cantonists," under which children from the age of twelve began to be conscripted into the army. Under a set quota, Jewish communities were required to supply ten recruits per thousand people (the quota for non-Jews was lower, and it was easier for them to exempt their children from conscription). The conscripted children were assigned by government officials — either placed in peasant homes or sent to special schools, where they remained until the age of eighteen, after which they were transferred to barracks, where they were required to serve for the next twenty-five years. This meant that children were torn away from home and cheder for a very long time, deliberately alienated from their people.No parent would willingly subject their child to such a cruel ordeal, but the community was obligated to fulfill the quota. This gave rise to the despicable trade of the "khapers" (catchers), whose job was to seize or kidnap children and hand them over to government officials. Heartbreaking scenes in which children were literally torn from their mothers' arms became commonplace.
texts.3: It was especially hard on the poorer segments of the Jewish population, who had no means to buy their children's freedom from the "khapers."Rabbi Menachem Mendel took up this problem with great energy, disregarding the possible threats and danger of the situation. It was necessary to save as many already-conscripted children as possible. To this end, the Rebbe formed a special council whose tasks were:1. To examine the situation of each Jewish community in order to help reduce the number of children it was required to send into military service.2. To take part in freeing children who had already been seized. This task was carried out by a secret society known as "Tachiyat HaMeitim" ("Reviving the Dead"). The main method of securing release was paying ransom to the officials involved in the matter. The latter would return the children while reporting to the authorities that they had died en route, and would also inform the relevant community of the boy's "death." These "death certificates" brought parents indescribable joy. The "deceased," of course, had to be hidden for a long time (hence the society's name), after which they were sent off to Talmud Torahs far from their home towns.3. To send trustworthy people to the places where the cantonist children were stationed, whose task was to offer them moral support and encourage them to remain faithful to their religion and their people.This activity involved not only enormous expense but also great danger, since it was tantamount to treason against the state. Nevertheless, this underground program was carried out successfully, and not a single case of betrayal was ever recorded.At the same time, Rabbi Menachem Mendel focused his efforts on supporting agricultural centers in the Vitebsk and Minsk areas. He sent one of the leading figures of the Chassidic movement, Rabbi Hillel of Paritch, on a tour of the settlements in the Kherson region.

**Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** (Yiddish: מנחם מענדל שניאורסאהן; September 20, 1789 – March 17, 1866), also known as the **Tzemach Tzedek** (Hebrew: "Righteous Sprout" or "Righteous Scion"), was an Orthodoxrabbi, leading 19th-century posek, and the third Rebbe (spiritual leader) of the Chabad LubavitchHasidic movement.

Menachem Mendel Schneersohn was born in Liozna, on September 20, 1789 (September 9 OS). His mother Devorah Leah died three years later, and her father Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi raised him as his own son. He married his first cousin Chaya Mushka Schneersohn, daughter of Rabbi Dovber Schneuri. After his father-in-law/uncle's death, and a three-year interregnum during which he tried to persuade the Hasidim to accept his brother-in-law Menachem-Nachum Schneuri or his uncle Chaim-Avraham as their leader,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) he assumed the leadership of Lubavitch on the eve of Shavuot 5591 (May 5, 1831, OS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-2)
He was known as the Tzemach Tzedek after the title of a voluminous compendium of Halakha (Jewish law) that he authored.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-3) He also authored _Derech Mitzvotecha_ ("Way of Your Commandments"), a mystical exposition of the _Mitzvos_. He compiled major works of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi for publication, including the _Siddur L'Kol Ha'Shanah_ (commonly known as _Siddur Im Dach_), _Likutei Torah_ and _Torah Ohr_. He also authored a philosophical text entitled _Sefer HaChakira: Derech Emunah_ (_Book of Philosophy: The Way of Faith_).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-4)

He enjoyed close ties with other Jewish leaders. In the course of his battle against the _Haskalah_ in Russia, he forged a close alliance with Rabbi Yitzchak of Valozhyn, a major leader of the misnagdim, which led to warmer relations between them and the Hasidim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-5)
According to Baruch Epstein, his father Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein spent six months under the Schneersohn's tutelage, and learned most of his mystical knowledge during that time. This story is disputed by Hassidic historian Yehoshua Mondshine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-6) Historian [Eitam Henkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Eitam_and_Na'ama_Henkin "Murder of Eitam and Na'ama Henkin") suggests that Rabbi Y. M. Epstein did meet with him, but only a few visits over a week or two, noting the testimony of Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maimon that he heard about this directly from his teacher.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-7)
His close friendship with Professor J Berstenson, the Czar's court physician, often helped the delicate negotiations relating to the welfare of the community.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) He set up an organisation called _Hevras Techiyas Hameisim_ to assist Jewish boy-soldiers who were being recruited and converted to Christianity by the Russian army. These soldiers known as Cantonists were taken away from the Jewish community to other villages. Schneersohn arranged for his students to pay them regular visits to keep up their spirits and discourage them from converting.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)

In 1844–45 he took steps to increase the enrollment and viability of the Lubavitch yeshivas in Dubroŭna, Pasana, Lyozno, and Kalisz, expanding their enrollment to around 600 students in total.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-8) Repeated attempts by the authorities to entrap him using informers such as Hershel Hodesh, Benjamin the Apostate and Lipman Feldman failed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-9)
He died in Lubavitch on March 17, 1866, at the age of 76, leaving seven sons. He was succeeded by his youngest son, Shmuel[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) as the Rebbe of Lubavitch, while several other sons established separate Chabad branches, including Kopust, Liadi, Niezhin and Avrutch.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)
Several of his sons established Chasidic dynasties.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)
He had seven sons:[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)

1. Rabbi Baruch Shalom (1805–1869) did not become a rebbe in his own right; he chose to remain in Lubavitch and become a chasid of his youngest brother. Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the seventh Rebbe of Chabad-Lubavitch, was his great-great-grandson.

2. Rabbi Yehuda Leib Schneersohn (Maharil) (1808–1866) settled in Kopys a few months after the death of his father, where he founded the Kopust branch of Chabad. He died two months later. He had three sons:

# **_Birth on a Sifting-Bed and an Unexpected Name_**
Towards three, the _Tzemach Tzedek_ again emerged from his room, his face radiant, telling the guests to lift up their spirits, for the _brit_ would definitely take place that day. With this he again returned to his room. Another hour went by. For the third time the _Tzemach Tzedek_ came out of his room, ordering the guests not yet to say the afternoon prayer as the _brit_ would take place momentarily. A little later he went to consult with his wife over the choice of a name for the child. He then ordered that the baby be readied, made his way to the synagogue, and the circumcision ceremony began.
During the course of the _brit milah_ the infant was crying a great deal. At a certain point, the _Tzemach Tzedek_, who was the _sandek_ holding the baby on his lap, removed his left hand from under the cushion and placed it on the tiny head. In that instant the crying stopped.
During the meal that followed, Rabbi Yehuda Leib, the son of the _Tzemach Tzedek_, asked his father: "For whom is the child named? As far as I know, no one in our family was ever called Shmuel. Does it concern the prophet Shmuel?" His father answered him: "He bears the name of a water-carrier from Polotsk who was called Shmuel - "A sage is superior to a prophet."
[Some say the water-carrier was one of the (36?) hidden _tzaddikim_.]
Elsewhere it is told that the Tzemach Tzedek said to the Rebbetzin:
"Shmuel the prophet came and asked me to give his name to the child, for 'I asked G-d for this child,' just as Chana, his mother, asked for Shmuel."

# **_Birth on a Sifting-Bed and an Unexpected Name_**
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Biographical notes: 

**Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** [of blessed memory: 29 Elul 5549 - 13 Nissan 5626 (Sept. 1789 - April 1866)], the third Rebbe of Chabad, was known as the **_Tzemach Tzedek_**, after his books of Jewish Law responsa and Talmudic commentary called by that name. **Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** (Yiddish: מנחם מענדל שניאורסאהן; September 20, 1789 – March 17, 1866), also known as the **Tzemach Tzedek** (Hebrew: "Righteous Sprout" or "Righteous Scion"), was an Orthodoxrabbi, leading 19th-century posek, and the third Rebbe (spiritual leader) of the Chabad LubavitchHasidic movement.
texts.1:
Menachem Mendel Schneersohn was born in Liozna, on September 20, 1789 (September 9 OS). His mother Devorah Leah died three years later, and her father Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi raised him as his own son. He married his first cousin Chaya Mushka Schneersohn, daughter of Rabbi Dovber Schneuri. After his father-in-law/uncle's death, and a three-year interregnum during which he tried to persuade the Hasidim to accept his brother-in-law Menachem-Nachum Schneuri or his uncle Chaim-Avraham as their leader,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) he assumed the leadership of Lubavitch on the eve of Shavuot 5591 (May 5, 1831, OS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-2)
He was known as the Tzemach Tzedek after the title of a voluminous compendium of Halakha (Jewish law) that he authored.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-3) He also authored _Derech Mitzvotecha_ ("Way of Your Commandments"), a mystical exposition of the _Mitzvos_. He compiled major works of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi for publication, including the _Siddur L'Kol Ha'Shanah_ (commonly known as _Siddur Im Dach_), _Likutei Torah_ and _Torah Ohr_. He also authored a philosophical text entitled _Sefer HaChakira: Derech Emunah_ (_Book of Philosophy: The Way of Faith_).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-4)
texts.2:
He enjoyed close ties with other Jewish leaders. In the course of his battle against the _Haskalah_ in Russia, he forged a close alliance with Rabbi Yitzchak of Valozhyn, a major leader of the misnagdim, which led to warmer relations between them and the Hasidim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-5)
According to Baruch Epstein, his father Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein spent six months under the Schneersohn's tutelage, and learned most of his mystical knowledge during that time. This story is disputed by Hassidic historian Yehoshua Mondshine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-6) Historian [Eitam Henkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Eitam_and_Na'ama_Henkin "Murder of Eitam and Na'ama Henkin") suggests that Rabbi Y. M. Epstein did meet with him, but only a few visits over a week or two, noting the testimony of Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maimon that he heard about this directly from his teacher.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-7)
His close friendship with Professor J Berstenson, the Czar's court physician, often helped the delicate negotiations relating to the welfare of the community.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) He set up an organisation called _Hevras Techiyas Hameisim_ to assist Jewish boy-soldiers who were being recruited and converted to Christianity by the Russian army. These soldiers known as Cantonists were taken away from the Jewish community to other villages. Schneersohn arranged for his students to pay them regular visits to keep up their spirits and discourage them from converting.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)
texts.3:
In 1844–45 he took steps to increase the enrollment and viability of the Lubavitch yeshivas in Dubroŭna, Pasana, Lyozno, and Kalisz, expanding their enrollment to around 600 students in total.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-8) Repeated attempts by the authorities to entrap him using informers such as Hershel Hodesh, Benjamin the Apostate and Lipman Feldman failed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-9)
He died in Lubavitch on March 17, 1866, at the age of 76, leaving seven sons. He was succeeded by his youngest son, Shmuel[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) as the Rebbe of Lubavitch, while several other sons established separate Chabad branches, including Kopust, Liadi, Niezhin and Avrutch.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)
Several of his sons established Chasidic dynasties.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)
He had seven sons:[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)

# **_Birth on a Sifting-Bed and an Unexpected Name_**
Towards three, the _Tzemach Tzedek_ again emerged from his room, his face radiant, telling the guests to lift up their spirits, for the _brit_ would definitely take place that day. With this he again returned to his room. Another hour went by. For the third time the _Tzemach Tzedek_ came out of his room, ordering the guests not yet to say the afternoon prayer as the _brit_ would take place momentarily. A little later he went to consult with his wife over the choice of a name for the child. He then ordered that the baby be readied, made his way to the synagogue, and the circumcision ceremony began.
During the course of the _brit milah_ the infant was crying a great deal. At a certain point, the _Tzemach Tzedek_, who was the _sandek_ holding the baby on his lap, removed his left hand from under the cushion and placed it on the tiny head. In that instant the crying stopped.
During the meal that followed, Rabbi Yehuda Leib, the son of the _Tzemach Tzedek_, asked his father: "For whom is the child named? As far as I know, no one in our family was ever called Shmuel. Does it concern the prophet Shmuel?" His father answered him: "He bears the name of a water-carrier from Polotsk who was called Shmuel - "A sage is superior to a prophet."
[Some say the water-carrier was one of the (36?) hidden _tzaddikim_.]
Elsewhere it is told that the Tzemach Tzedek said to the Rebbetzin:
"Shmuel the prophet came and asked me to give his name to the child, for 'I asked G-d for this child,' just as Chana, his mother, asked for Shmuel."

We need to answer: "Who did the creator of Derech Mitzvosecha follow?" So question: "Who did the creator of Derech Mitzvosecha follow?" means: The author of Derech Mitzvosecha is Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (Tzemach Tzedek). Who did he follow? In context of Chabad perhaps? He followed his grandfather, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi (the Alter Rebbe). He might have followed Rabbi Shalom Shachna? The question likely from Dovverts or Suza: "Who did the creator of Derech Mitzvosecha follow?" It may refer to his spiritual mentor: He was followed by the same tradition of Chabad following the teachings of Shneur Zalman. The creator likely followed the teachings of his grandfather, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liozna. Or he followed the Rebbe's chain: He followed the Talmudic tradition, but more likely "he followed Rabbi Shalom Shachna"?? Hmm.

Maybe the question refers to the concept of "following" in Chassidic sense: "Who did the creator... follow?" The creator is the Tzemach Tzedek, who followed his grandfather. According to sources: He was raised by his grandfather, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, who taught him Torah and Chabad philosophy. So answer: He followed his grandfather, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, the founder of Chabad. Also he followed the Rebbe's teachings of Chabad.

The Chasidic classic Derech Mitzvosecha, by Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch also known as the Tzemach Tzedek, the third Lubavitcher Rebbe (5549 [1789] – 5626 [1866]) translated to English.
R. Menachem Mendel composed this work in his early adulthood. It focuses on many of the 613 mitzvos of the Torah. The Tzemach Tzedek begins his treatment of each mitzvah by quoting the Sefer Hachinuch, the landmark work that lists all 613 mitzvos and their motivating rationales. Occasionally, it cites other sources in Nigleh and briefly outlines the mystical secrets the Kabbalah associates with this Mitzvah. afterwards, he explains these ideas within the context of Chassidus and in the course of doing so, provides his readers with many fundamental concepts applicable in their Divine service.
Included in this volume:
*   Issur Sinas Yisrael, Mitzvas Ahavas Yisrael   
*   Mitzvas Vidui U’Teshuvah

*   Mitzvas Kiddush HaShem

*   Mitzvas Binyan Mikdash   
*   Mitzvas Tzitzis

The Chasidic classic Derech Mitzvosecha, by Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch also known as the Tzemach Tzedek, the third Lubavitcher Rebbe (5549 [1789] – 5626 [1866]) translated to English.
R. Menachem Mendel composed this work in his early adulthood. It focuses on many of the 613 mitzvos of the Torah. The Tzemach Tzedek begins his treatment of each mitzvah by quoting the Sefer Hachinuch, the landmark work that lists all 613 mitzvos and their motivating rationales. Occasionally, it cites other sources in Nigleh and briefly outlines the mystical secrets the Kabbalah associates with this Mitzvah. afterwards, he explains these ideas within the context of Chassidus and in the course of doing so, provides his readers with many fundamental concepts applicable in their Divine service.

steps.reasoning: The question: "Who did the creator of Derech Mitzvosecha follow?" Means: who did the creator of Derech Mitzvosecha follow? Creator is Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn, the Tzemach Tzedek. Who did he follow? Likely his teacher, his mentor? He was a disciple of his grandfather Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi (the Talmidei of the Chabad movement). But perhaps the question refers to "who did he follow" as someone he studied under or followed spiritually? Let's search for "Menachem Mendel Schneersohn followed by whom" or "followed the Chassidic teacher".

**Menachem Mendel Schneerson**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-1) (April 18[O.S. April 5]1902 – June 12, 1994), known to adherents of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement as **the Lubavitcher Rebbe** or simply **the Rebbe**,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-3) was an Orthodox rabbi, alleged Messiah claimant, and the Rebbe of the Lubavitch Hasidic dynasty. He is considered one of the most influential Jewish leaders of the 20th century.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-nytimes.com-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-5)
As leader of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement, he took an insular Hasidic group that almost came to an end with the Holocaust and transformed it into one of the most influential movements in religious Jewry,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-6) with an international network of over 5,000 educational and social centers.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-jns.org-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-9) The institutions he established include kindergartens, schools, drug-rehabilitation centers, care homes for disabled people, and synagogues.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-observer.com-10)

Schneerson's published teachings fill more than 400 volumes, and he is noted for his contributions to Jewish continuity and religious thought,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-11) as well as his wide-ranging contributions to traditional Torah scholarship.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-ou.org-12) He is recognized as the pioneer of Jewish outreach.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-jewishfederations.org-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Susan-14) During his lifetime, many of his adherents believed that he was the Messiah, though not all Chabadniks subscribe to this belief. His own attitude to the subject, and whether he proclaimed it, is hotly debated among academics and scholars of Judaism. During Schneerson's lifetime, the messianic controversy and other issues elicited fierce criticism from many quarters in the Orthodox world, from Israel's Chief RabbiOvadia Yosef to Elazar Shach.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-15)

In 1978, the U.S. Congress asked President Jimmy Carter to designate Schneerson's birthday as the national Education Day in the U.S.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Wikisource-16) It has been since commemorated as Education and Sharing Day.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-18) In 1994, Schneerson was posthumously awarded the Congressional Gold Medal for his "outstanding and lasting contributions toward improvements in world education, morality, and acts of charity".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Public_Law_103-457-19)Schneerson's resting place attracts Jews for prayer.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Sarah_Maslin_Nir_2013-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-21)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-observer.com-10)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-tabletmag.com-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Shepherd-23)

### Early life and education
[edit]
Menachem Mendel Schneerson was born on April 18, 1902 (April 5, 1902 OS; 11 Nisan, AM 5662), in the Black Sea port of Nikolaev in the Russian Empire (now Mykolaiv in Ukraine).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Telushkin455-24) His father was rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson, a renowned Talmudic scholar and authority on Kabbalah and Jewish law.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-25) His mother was RebbetzinChana Schneerson (née Yanovski). He was named after the third Chabad rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneersohn, the _Tzemach Tzedek_, from whom he was a direct patrilineal descendant.
In 1907, when Schneerson was five years old, the family moved to Yekaterinoslav, where Levi Yitzchak was appointed Chief Rabbi of the city. He served until 1939, when he was exiled by the Soviets for five years to Kazakhstan[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-26) for his activities on behalf of strengthening Judaism in the Soviet Union. Schneerson had two younger brothers: Dov Ber Schneerson, who was murdered in 1944 by Nazi collaborators, and Yisroel Aryeh Leib Schneerson, who died in 1952 while completing doctoral studies at Liverpool University.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Telushkin455-24)

### Marriage and family life
In 1991, a car in convoy with Schneerson's motorcade accidentally struck two Guyanese American children while running a red light. One of the children was killed. The incident triggered the Crown Heights riot.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-81)

### Seventh Chabad Rebbe
[edit]
The AshkenaziChief Rabbis of Israel, Avraham Elkana Kahana Shapira and Mordechai Eliyahu at the Lubavitcher rebbe on the 11th of Iyar 5749 (May 16, 1989)
After the death of Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn in 1950, Chabad followers began persuading Schneerson to succeed his father-in-law as Rebbe, citing his scholarship, piety, and dynasty.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-:0-82)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-chabad-83) Schneerson was reluctant, and refused to accept leadership of the movement. He continued, however, with all the communal activities he had previously headed. It would take a full year for the elders to persuade him to join the movement in accepting the post.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-84)

### Seventh Chabad Rebbe
On the first anniversary (yahrzeit) of his father-in-law's passing, 10 Shevat 5711 (January 17, 1951),[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-85) Schneerson took on the role at a ceremony attended by several hundred rabbis and Jewish leaders from all parts of the United States and Canada. He delivered a Hasidic discourse _(Ma'amar)_, the equivalent to a President-elect taking the oath of office, and formally became the Rebbe.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-86) In the ma’amar, known as "Bosi L'gani" (I have come into My garden), the Rebbe stated his mission: to bring the Messiah ("Moshiach"). On the night of his acceptance, members of the Israeli Cabinet and the Chief Rabbi of Israel, Yitzhak HaLevi Herzog, sent him congratulatory messages.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-87)
Reiterating a longstanding core Chabad principle at his inaugural talk, he demanded that each individual exert themselves in advancing spiritually and _not_ rely on the Rebbe to do it for them, saying:
> Now listen, Jews. Generally, in Chabad, it has been demanded that each work on themselves, and not rely on the Rebbes. One must, _on their own_, transform the folly of materialism and the passion of the 'animal soul' to holiness. I do not, God Forbid, recuse myself from assisting as much as possible, however; if one does not work on _themselves_, what good will submitting notes, singing songs, and saying lechayim do?[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-88)

### Seventh Chabad Rebbe
At the same talk, Schneerson said, "one must go to a place where nothing is known of Godliness, nothing is known of Judaism, nothing is even known of the Hebrew alphabet, and while there to put oneself aside and ensure that the other calls out to God."[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-89) When he spoke to _The Forward_ journalist Asher Penn that year, he said, "...we must stop insisting that Judaism is in danger, an assertion that does little but place Jewry on the defensive. We need to go on the offensive."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-90)
Aharon Daum (center) talks with the Rebbe (right) during the distribution of dollars for charity.

### Seventh Chabad Rebbe
As Rebbe, Schneerson would receive visitors for private meetings, known as _yechidus_, on Sunday and Thursday evenings. Those meetings would begin at 8 pm and often continue until 5 or 6 in the morning, and were open to everyone.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-chabad-83)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Weiner,_Herbert_page_158-91) Schneerson, who spoke several languages including English, Yiddish, Hebrew, Aramaic, French, Russian, German, and Italian, would converse with people on all issues and offer his advice on both spiritual and mundane matters.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-worldof237-92) Politicians and leaders from across the globe came to meet him, but Schneerson showed no preference for one person over another. His secretary once even declined to admit John F. Kennedy because Schneerson was already meeting people who had requested appointments months previously.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-observer.com-10) Those meetings were discontinued in 1982, when it became impossible to accommodate many people. Meetings were then held only for those with a special occasion, such as a bride and groom for a wedding or a boy and his family for a bar mitzvah.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-worldof237-92)

### Seventh Chabad Rebbe
During his four decades as Rebbe, Schneerson would deliver regular addresses centered on the weekly Torah portion and on various tractates of the Talmud. These talks, delivered without text or notes, would last for several hours,[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-The_Depth_p.201-93)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-94) and sometimes went for eight or nine hours without a break. During the talks, Schneerson demonstrated a unique approach to explaining seemingly different concepts by analyzing the fundamental principle common to the entire tractate.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-95)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-97) and referenced both classic and esoteric sources from all periods, citing entire sections by heart.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-The_Depth_p.201-93)

### Outreach, spiritual campaigns
[edit]
In 1951, Schneerson established a Chabad women's and girl's organization and a youth organization in Israel. Their mission was to engage in outreach exclusively directed at women and teens. In 1953, he opened branches of these organizations in New York, London, and Toronto. Schneerson equally addressed his teachings to both genders in a marked departure from an entrenched tendency to limit high-level Torah education to men and boys.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-98) He addressed meetings of the organizations and led gatherings exclusively for women. Schneerson would describe the increase in Torah study by women as one of the "positive innovations of the later generations".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-99)

### Outreach, spiritual campaigns
#### Sunday office hours for charity
[edit]
In 1986, Schneerson began a custom where, each Sunday, he would stand outside his office, greet people briefly, give them a dollar bill, and encourage them to donate it to the charity of their choice.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Hoff47-115) Explaining his reason for encouraging charitable giving among all people, Schneerson quoted his father-in-law, who said that "when two people meet, it should bring benefit to a third."[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-116) People in line would often take this opportunity to ask Schneerson for advice or request a blessing. Thousands of people attended this event each week, which lasted up to six hours, and is often referred to as "Sunday Dollars".[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-117)
Schneerson's wife, Chaya Mushka Schneerson, died in 1988.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Chaya_Schneerson-43) During the week of _shiva_, Schneerson wrote a will in which he bequeathed his entire estate to Agudas Chasidei Chabad, the Chabad umbrella organization.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-118)

### Outreach, spiritual campaigns
#### Sunday office hours for charity
During a talk in 1991, Schneerson spoke passionately about Moshiach (the Messiah) and told his followers that he had done all that he could bring world peace and redemption but that it was now up to them to continue this task: "I have done my part, from now on you do all that you can." A few months later, when a reporter from CNN came to meet him at a Sunday Dollars, he said, "Moshiach is ready to come now; it is only on our part to do something additional in the realm of goodness and kindness."[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-119)

### Outreach, spiritual campaigns
#### His message: become righteous
[edit]
On Sunday, March 1, 1992, Gabriel Erem, the editor of _Lifestyles Magazine_, told Schneerson that on his ninetieth birthday, they would be publishing a special issue and wanted to know his message to the world. Schneerson replied that "'Ninety', in Hebrew, is _tzaddik_; which means 'righteous.' And that is a direct indication for every person to become a real _tzaddik_—a righteous person, and to do so for many years, until 120. This message applies equally to Jews and non-Jews".[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-120)
During his decades of leadership, Schneerson worked over 18 hours a day and never took a day of vacation.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-121) He rarely left Brooklyn except for visits to his father-in-law's gravesite in Queens, New York. Schneerson opposed retirement, seeing it as a waste of precious years.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-122) In 1972, on the occasion of his 70th birthday, instead of announcing a retirement plan, Schneerson proposed the establishment of 71 new institutions to mark the beginning of the 71st year of his life.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-123) The only other time he left Brooklyn was when he visited Camp Gan IsraelParksville, New York in 1956, 1957 and 1960.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-124)

### Outreach, spiritual campaigns
#### His message: become righteous
In 1977, during the _hakafot_ ceremony on Shemini Atzeret, Schneerson suffered a heart attack. At his request, rather than transporting him to a hospital, the doctors set up a mini-hospital at his office where he was treated for the next four weeks by doctors Bernard Lown, Ira Weiss, and Larry Resnick.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-125) He made a full recovery from the heart attack with few, if any, noticeable lasting effects or changes to his work habits. Fifteen years later, Schneerson suffered a serious stroke while praying at the grave of his father-in-law. The stroke left him unable to speak and paralyzed on the right side of his body. The hope that Schneerson could be revealed as the Messiah became more widespread during this time.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-wp06201999-126)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Gonzalez-127)

### Outreach, spiritual campaigns
#### His message: become righteous
On the morning of June 12, 1994, Schneerson died at the Beth Israel Medical Center in New York city, and was buried at the Ohel next to his father-in-law, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, at Montefiore Cemetery in Queens, New York.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-128)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-NYT19940613A1-129) Shortly after Schneerson's death, the executors of his will discovered several notebooks in a drawer in his office, in which Schneerson had written his scholarly thoughts and religious musings from his earliest years.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Gonzalez-127) The majority of entries in these journals date between 1928 and 1950 and were subsequently published.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-130)
Schneerson's burial place next to his father-in-law and predecessor in Queens, New York

### Outreach, spiritual campaigns
#### His message: become righteous
Following age-old Jewish tradition that the grave of a tzadik is holy, Schneerson's gravesite is viewed by many as a sacred site. It has been described by _Yedioth Ahronoth_ as "the American Western Wall", where thousands of Jews[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-observer.com-10) go to pray each week.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-tabletmag.com-22)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-131)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-Sarah_Maslin_Nir_2013-20) Many more send faxes and e-mails with requests for prayers to be read at the gravesite.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneerson#cite_note-132)

**Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** (Yiddish: מנחם מענדל שניאורסאהן; September 20, 1789 – March 17, 1866), also known as the **Tzemach Tzedek** (Hebrew: "Righteous Sprout" or "Righteous Scion"), was an Orthodoxrabbi, leading 19th-century posek, and the third Rebbe (spiritual leader) of the Chabad LubavitchHasidic movement.

Menachem Mendel Schneersohn was born in Liozna, on September 20, 1789 (September 9 OS). His mother Devorah Leah died three years later, and her father Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi raised him as his own son. He married his first cousin Chaya Mushka Schneersohn, daughter of Rabbi Dovber Schneuri. After his father-in-law/uncle's death, and a three-year interregnum during which he tried to persuade the Hasidim to accept his brother-in-law Menachem-Nachum Schneuri or his uncle Chaim-Avraham as their leader,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) he assumed the leadership of Lubavitch on the eve of Shavuot 5591 (May 5, 1831, OS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-2)
He was known as the Tzemach Tzedek after the title of a voluminous compendium of Halakha (Jewish law) that he authored.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-3) He also authored _Derech Mitzvotecha_ ("Way of Your Commandments"), a mystical exposition of the _Mitzvos_. He compiled major works of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi for publication, including the _Siddur L'Kol Ha'Shanah_ (commonly known as _Siddur Im Dach_), _Likutei Torah_ and _Torah Ohr_. He also authored a philosophical text entitled _Sefer HaChakira: Derech Emunah_ (_Book of Philosophy: The Way of Faith_).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-4)

He enjoyed close ties with other Jewish leaders. In the course of his battle against the _Haskalah_ in Russia, he forged a close alliance with Rabbi Yitzchak of Valozhyn, a major leader of the misnagdim, which led to warmer relations between them and the Hasidim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-5)
According to Baruch Epstein, his father Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein spent six months under the Schneersohn's tutelage, and learned most of his mystical knowledge during that time. This story is disputed by Hassidic historian Yehoshua Mondshine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-6) Historian [Eitam Henkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Eitam_and_Na'ama_Henkin "Murder of Eitam and Na'ama Henkin") suggests that Rabbi Y. M. Epstein did meet with him, but only a few visits over a week or two, noting the testimony of Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maimon that he heard about this directly from his teacher.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-7)
His close friendship with Professor J Berstenson, the Czar's court physician, often helped the delicate negotiations relating to the welfare of the community.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) He set up an organisation called _Hevras Techiyas Hameisim_ to assist Jewish boy-soldiers who were being recruited and converted to Christianity by the Russian army. These soldiers known as Cantonists were taken away from the Jewish community to other villages. Schneersohn arranged for his students to pay them regular visits to keep up their spirits and discourage them from converting.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)

In 1844–45 he took steps to increase the enrollment and viability of the Lubavitch yeshivas in Dubroŭna, Pasana, Lyozno, and Kalisz, expanding their enrollment to around 600 students in total.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-8) Repeated attempts by the authorities to entrap him using informers such as Hershel Hodesh, Benjamin the Apostate and Lipman Feldman failed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-9)
He died in Lubavitch on March 17, 1866, at the age of 76, leaving seven sons. He was succeeded by his youngest son, Shmuel[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) as the Rebbe of Lubavitch, while several other sons established separate Chabad branches, including Kopust, Liadi, Niezhin and Avrutch.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)
Several of his sons established Chasidic dynasties.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)
He had seven sons:[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)

1. Rabbi Baruch Shalom (1805–1869) did not become a rebbe in his own right; he chose to remain in Lubavitch and become a chasid of his youngest brother. Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the seventh Rebbe of Chabad-Lubavitch, was his great-great-grandson.
